item.title: God, Death, Beauty, and Other Ultimate Concerns in Therapy
item.description:
Therapy

God, Death, Beauty, and Other Ultimate Concerns in Therapy

Why our most soulful concerns matter too much to be ignored in psychotherapy.

Posted August 17, 2026

Key points
  • Psychotherapy needs to be receptive to a patient's ultimate concerns like beauty, spirituality, and mortality.
  • The patient's symptoms sometimes stem from conflicts regarding their ultimate concerns.
  • The reality of evil is another often-unacknowledged ultimate concern in therapy.

Existential theologian and philosopher Paul Tillich (1952) spoke of our "ultimate concerns," those things that most truly and passionately matter to and motivate us, providing our lives with a profound sense of commitment, meaning, and purpose. Ultimate concerns influence our values, choices, and actions, though we sometimes refuse to admit to or deny having them, even to ourselves. Ultimate concerns, when consciously acknowledged and courageously confirmed, can imbue existence with a newfound sense of meaning, purpose, significance, and direction. This is why exploring and clarifying our ultimate concerns is not only appropriate but an essential task in psychotherapy.

However, most modern psychotherapy is relatively brief, symptom-focused, pragmatic, goal-oriented, technique-driven, manualized, and exclusively concerned with specifically addressing the patient's presenting problems, symptoms, or complaints and nothing else. Once these presenting signs and symptoms—which are considered by both the clinician and patient as being their primary concern—have been reduced or eliminated, typically today with the help of some psychopharmacological intervention, the patient is sent packing (see my previous post). But what happens when the patient spontaneously and, to some therapists, superfluously starts speaking in session not of their difficulties at work, nor of their distressing anxiety or depression symptoms, but rather of more esoteric subjects like loneliness, beauty, God, death, or the problem of evil? Is this still psychotherapy?

Should Spiritual and Existential Questions Be Included in Therapy?

Some today might say such soulful subjects are inappropriate and irrelevant to therapy—perhaps even taboo. But I wonder whether any mental health treatment that excludes, dismisses, or devalues such basic spiritual or existential questions and concerns can or should be considered real psychotherapy, since these archetypal ultimate concerns commonly, whether consciously or unconsciously, explicitly or implicitly, comprise the very heart and soul of what therapy is really all about: helping people to discern and discover what truly matters to them and provides their lives with meaning, purpose, and significance. Therapy is about accompanying clients or patients through and, whenever pragmatically possible, beyond their mundane problems and symptoms to recognizing and embracing their ultimate concerns, accepting their fate, and finding and fulfilling their personal destiny. Or, at least, setting them on that path. This, it seems to me, is a far cry from what typically passes for psychotherapy today.

Finding, appreciating, or creating beauty is one such ultimate concern. We all need and seek some beauty to offset and counterbalance the pervasive ugliness in life: the existential reality of evil, loss, suffering, tragedy, disease, and death. In his semi-autobiographical book My Quest for Beauty (1985), psychologist Rollo May relates his own rediscovery of beauty and its rejuvenating power. Finding himself as a young man alone in a foreign culture for the first time and in the throes of what he himself calls a "nervous breakdown," May, while wandering aimlessly in the hills of Greece, suddenly comes upon a gorgeous sea of wild poppies and experiences a life-altering epiphany: "I realized that I had not listened to my inner voice, which had tried to talk to me about beauty. I had been too hard-working, too ‘principled' to spend time merely looking at flowers! It seems it had taken a collapse of my whole former way of life for this voice to make itself heard." This reawakening to his ultimate concern about beauty helped lift him out of his despair and propelled him toward a new, more authentic, creative, vital life, eventually becoming a psychotherapist.

Losing Touch With Ultimate Concerns in Modern Life

This is sometimes a problem with psychotherapy patients today. They have lost touch with their transcendent sense of beauty or with their other ultimate concerns such as spirituality, helping or healing humanity, creativity, etc., because of being so preoccupied with and focused on their own symptoms and problems. May (1985) shares the following excerpt from a memorable therapy session with a patient he was seeing at his home in the hills above San Francisco Bay, who, up to this point, had been totally focused on her mundane marital problems. But, one day, seemingly out of the blue, she sat down as usual in her session and said this: "I stopped my car on the way here to look at the twilight. It was just beautiful, the purple hues with green hills, behind them ... It is the most beautiful time of day ... I don't believe in a God, at least in a personal God, there is so much evil in the world, it makes it so pointless. But when I see such beauty, I can't believe it is by accident ... This time of day would be a good time to die, a good time to be alone ... I would like to die at this time ... It is so peaceful here in your office ... I keep noticing the beauty outside the window."

Now, some might find this patient's spontaneous, seemingly off-topic talk of beauty, God, death, and evil irrelevant, alarming, or perhaps interpret it as her "resistance" to therapy. Indeed, the patient herself, toward the end of the session, recounts May, "expressed her fear that she had said nothing today, maybe it was all superficial talk." But rather than confirming her fears, writes May, "I assured her that no topics could be more important than beauty, God, death." What exactly did he mean by that cryptic comment? May meant, I suspect, that psychotherapy, real psychotherapy, is not merely some technical process or series of psychological, cognitive, or behavioral interventions to correct, "fix," or eliminate people's symptoms—which are almost always symptomatic of some underlying conflict—but is ultimately concerned with helping patients to become more fully present to, aware, or conscious and accepting of themselves, others, the world, existential reality, and their own ultimate concerns, whatever they may be. At its best, psychotherapy provides patients the opportunity, if and when appropriate, to grapple with these thorny questions and concerns, which are frequently closely connected to their presenting problems, complaints, or symptoms.

The Therapeutic Value of Addressing Ultimate Concerns

But what, you may ask, do such obscure philosophical or spiritual musings in therapy have to do with ameliorating or alleviating the patient's symptoms and suffering as quickly and expediently as possible? And, why bother, since with some psychiatric medication and cognitive-behavioral therapy we can ameliorate or at least mitigate the patient's symptoms in relatively short order? We live today in a therapeutic culture that devalues and avoids speaking or even thinking of such things. Indeed, in our day, psychotherapy patients sadly are implicitly or explicitly discouraged to discuss or dwell deeply on such impertinent matters. But if practitioners and patients can recognize and respect the pragmatic therapeutic power, relevance, value, significance, and profound importance of acknowledging and addressing our ultimate concerns—creativity, beauty, evil, loneliness, meaninglessness, suffering, freedom, responsibility, fate, destiny, spirituality, and death—during therapy, then perhaps this sort of soulful psychotherapy has some chance of surviving.

item.title: 4 Signs That Interactions at Work Are Toxic
item.description:
Career

4 Signs That Interactions at Work Are Toxic

How to tell when discussions at work are destructive and what to do about it.

Posted August 17, 2026

Key points
  • Knowing the signs of a toxic work interaction can help you protect yourself.
  • Signs include a person who doesn't perspective-take and who distort things or attacks your character.
  • After identifying a discussion as destructive, set a boundary to protect yourself moving forward.

Working out conflict with those around you is healthy and necessary. Yet, when things escalate and the conversation turns sideways, you regret bringing anything up. Instead of getting a resolution or compromise, you are hurt, and the relationship seems damaged. Know the four signs of a discussion that is destructive and free yourself from these dreadful conversations. Then, learn what to do instead.

1. Lack of Perspective-Taking in Conversations

First, the talk is absent of perspective-taking by one or more of the people involved. Meaning, your thoughts and feelings are instantly dismissed, and the person launches into a diatribe about their opinion on the matter. You may continue to try explaining your viewpoint, but the same thing happens. The other person immediately cuts you off and takes 20 minutes talking about why they are correct. You barely get a word in edgewise. To be heard, you get louder and more animated, but it is useless. Then, this person uses your intensity against you and accuses you of having anger issues and of constantly interrupting them.

2. Intellectualization to Avoid Emotions

Second, they intellectualize. Intellectualization is an unconscious defense mechanism that protects people from having to grapple with their uncomfortable emotions, like empathy. During this discussion, the person asserts that their argument is superior because it is rational and based in fact. This allows them to forgo empathizing with you or anyone else and prevents you from identifying important relational dynamics that need to be handled.

For example, Rachel confronts her friend and co-worker, Sarah, because she discovered that Sarah poached some of her customers behind her back. Sarah is offended at the suggestion that she did something wrong. She states, “This is business. This is not personal. I have higher credentials and more experience than you. Period. End of story.” Sarah does not acknowledge that she was manipulative or unfair to Sarah and that Sarah has a right to be upset. Instead, she justifies her actions with a logical response based in “facts.”

3. Distorting and Rewriting History

Third, the person distorts things. They rewrite history, or they skew things to benefit their argument. As the debate goes on, they twist things to position themselves as innocent or the victim in the situation, and you as the aggressor.

For example, Taylor and Rick are friends who also work together. Taylor enters his office and immediately notices that his ergonomically correct chair has been replaced with an ordinary one. He walks past Rick’s office and sees Rick sitting in his chair. He stops in the doorway and asks, “Did you take my chair?” Surprised, Rick looks up and says that Taylor gave him permission to swap their chairs a few weeks ago. Yet, Taylor has no recollection of this. Rick is adamant and launches into a long story about how badly his back hurts from the bike accident. Taylor is really confused because he and Rick laughed about the funny and harmless incident on the bike trail, and Rick has never complained about back pain. Rick insinuates that Taylor is a bad friend for not supporting him with his injury. Confused, Taylor questions his own listening skills and memory.

4. Attacking Character Instead of Addressing Issues

Fourth, the person attacks your character instead of sticking to the material being discussed. They switch gears and blame you for the incident because of your “poor character.”

For example, Becky recognizes her team is missing a template for a service that they provide for customers. She spends time creating a document for the team that they can use to avoid any misunderstandings in the future. She runs it by Lisa to make sure it covers what they need. Lisa looks at it and asks Becky why it was not done sooner. Becky acknowledges her point and says, “It will make things easier for us in the future.” Lisa scoffs and says, “If you knew what you were doing, this would’ve been done months ago. You just don’t have good business sense.” Becky feels like she just got punched in the gut, but she lets the comment go, and tells Lisa that the document will be available ASAP.

If these four things occur when you are having a discussion with someone, it may not be worth it because they will not see your point anyways. It is a waste of breath. Moreover, you get upset, question your sanity, and incur emotional mistreatment that impacts your self-esteem. It may be better to have empathy for yourself, mourn the loss of a relationship that you thought was safe and trusted, and set a boundary to prevent the issue from occurring again.

How to Respond

Rachel sets a boundary by adding to her spiel with a new customer. If it feels like a good match, she says, “If at any point, I fail to meet your needs, and you’d like to transfer to a new representative, please let me know. I want you to be happy. I can facilitate the change in a timely manner, which means you won’t have a lag in service.” This simple phrase informs the client of the proper process if they are approached by Sarah… without ever mentioning her. If Sarah does approach them, they may see her as sneaky and possibly even unprofessional.

Taylor remains warm and friendly toward Rick, but orders a new office chair and avoids discussions with Rick unless other trusted colleagues are around. He may need verification of what was said. He also locks his office door when he leaves at night.

Becky sets a boundary by not going to Lisa in the future for feedback. She hires a business consultant for this. She’s pleasant to Lisa but utilizes her professional consultant for important matters.

Although it is difficult to believe that some people are not trustworthy, it is important data to know, especially so you can protect yourself. Avoid toxic discussions when you can and think creatively about setting a boundary that protects you in the future. You can find more information on the topic in my book, How to Outsmart a Narcissist; Use Emotional Intelligence to Regain Control at Home, at Work, and In Life.
